articles.text: It looks now as though women would be granted the right of suffrage in Dakota. There is but little opposition to the bill and it seems as though the majority of the legislature are in favor of it. On account of the crankiness of the leaders of the womans' rights movement the subject has always been a matter of mirth rather than a serious one. Practical experience has shown, however, that women are as well qualified to vote as men and we hope to see the measure pass.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy predicts Dakota will grant woman suffrage and says it hopes the measure passes.

articles.text: The Union News, of Union, N. Y. is the last tenderfoot sheet that has come to the front. The last issue contains the notice that snow is twenty to twenty-five feet deep in Montana. We do not think there is a place in Montana or Dakota where there has been even two feet on a level and only in exceptional cases has it reached a depth of eighteen inches. We merely make these remarks to show the animos of the eastern press toward the northwest. On every occasion they will publish articles such as the one referred to, knowing, if the editors have any sense, that they are entirely devoid of truth.
articles.summary: The paper rebuts an eastern report of 20-25 feet of snow in Montana, saying snow has nowhere reached two feet on a level.

articles.text: We have seen a letter srom Mr. McCall, who introduced a bill for the repeal of the herd law, stating that no one has petitioned for the repeal from here, and that it might be as well not to exempt the Bad Lands here, as no one seems to wish it. This is enough to call for immediate action on the part of cattlemen here, and a man should be sent at once to Bismarck to present our side of the case. While in Bismarck recently we were convinced from conversations with legislators that the herd law could be repealed and we have so expressed ourselves in the Cow Boy. Now the matter may go by default unless immediate action is taken.
articles.summary: A letter from Mr. McCall, author of the herd-law repeal bill, says no Bad Lands petition for repeal has arrived; the Cow Boy urges cattlemen to send a man to Bismarck at once.

articles.text: The Dakota Blade, Jimmy Emmon's paper, is on the war path after corruption, but Jimmy has bitten off more than he can chew in attempting to show that the herd law should not be repealed for the Bad Lands, because farmers could not then come in. The truth of the matter is, that although Jimmy is well acquainted with the east Missouri country, he has never been in the Bad Lands, and does not realize that perpendicular farming does not pay. From the nature of the ground, farming to any extent is impossible in the Bad Lands, and as long as so much better farming land can be had farther east for the taking, there will be no hardship in a repeal of the herd law here.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy rebuts the Dakota Blade (Jimmy Emmons) on herd-law repeal, arguing farming is impossible in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: Experience although a dear teacher, seems to be about the only successful one, especially in cattle raising. From its teachings, however, two thing have, or ought to have been learned thoroughly. Never buy yearlings and never drive in cattle later than August. An exception might be made in favor of yearlings, in case they are brought in before June or July, but even in that case there is a far greater percentage of risk than it is necessary to take. There is scarcely a cattle man in the Bad Lands with whom we have not spoken on these two points and we think we are above the mark in estimating a loss of one per cent. on all two-year-olds and over on cattle landed here early, whether they are pilgrims or not. Two-thirds of the total loss will be on yearlings and cattle landed here late. A good illustration of this point are the V V V and B X B outfits, on the Belle Fouche. The V V V has lost but little on old cattle, the most of their loss coming on yearlings and late dogies. The B X B, with a corresponding location and a mixed herd which was driven in late in the fall, have been heavy losers on all classes of cattle. Of course any estimate of loss is pure guess-work, but there is no question that it would be nerely nominal had it not been for yearlings and late cattle.
articles.summary: Editorial advice never to buy yearlings or drive in cattle after August, citing winter losses of the VVV and BXB outfits on the Belle Fourche.

articles.text: An organization known as the International Arbeiter, or workingmen's association, has been holding secret meetings in Philadelphia for some time. A reporter of one of the papers joined the body, and exposed the workings of the organization. Johann Most and Justus Schwab are the leading spirits. At first there was difficulty in securing members, but of late the ranks have been swelled considerably. The object of this association seems to be to overthrow all law and build up a government of its own. It seems strange that any workingman, who has the slightest respect for himself or anyone else would join an organization of this kind. There are rights which workingmen have, and the best thing they can do is to exercise them in the best and most honorable ways. By joining such an order as the International Arbeiter he does not advance his interests one whit, but on the contrary, tends to lessen his chances for a fair deal. The leaders, Most and Schwab, are cranks on this subject, and are men whom every true workingmen should combine against. If a man joins a workingmen's protective association, let him join one he is not afraid to own publicly, in which all the members are on an equal footing, and not one lead by such men as are at the head of this body—who want everything their own way, though thousands of dollars worth of property are destroyed, or even at the price of blood. A workingman has the right to say he will work for so much and no less, but he cannot stop others from taking his place; nor has he the right to destroy his employer's property. Such proceedings cause bitter feelings between capital and labor, and it is to be hoped that the "men of toil" will learn this and prevent the spread of the International Arbeiter's association.
articles.summary: Editorial condemning the International Arbeiter association led by Johann Most and Justus Schwab in Philadelphia.

articles.text: One of the largest and most experienced breeders and raisers of horses in Illinois says that if you will give one or two mouthfuls of hay to the horse before you water him, there will never be any danger of the horse being water-founded. This is, as far as he knows, an infallible rule, and is worth being remembered by all horsemen.—[Ex.

articles.text: After all the fuss about cattle losses, it turns out that about the only loss amounting to much was in two or three counties south of San Antonio, where there is no grass and the cattle are very poor. And even in these counties the loss is greatly exagerated. Thanks to the prickly pear, the loss of cattle even there is much lighter than expected.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Texas cattle losses were confined to a few counties south of San Antonio.

articles.text: Our reports from the different ranges of the territory are veay much alike. All agree that up to the present time there has not been much loss of stock, if any; but also all agree that unless we have fairly good weather from this out the loss is likely to make one feel uncomfortable. There is no use denying the fact that during the past 50 days stock has suffered much.—[Stock and Mining Journal.
articles.summary: Montana ranges report little loss so far but stock has suffered in the past 50 days.

articles.text: The building of wind breaks on the range has been suggested by a cattlemen who thinks that the expense would not be very great and that it would keep cattle from drifting. The breaks could be built of sod, stone or lumber, in a straight line, so that cattle could seek shelter on either side. Where the herds are not too large the plan would work very well.—[Globe L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Suggestion to build wind breaks on the range to stop cattle drifting.

articles.text: Cross-breds are coming to the front as prize winners. Everyone has become so accustomed to thinking some particular breed is the best, that the fact of every one coming from the same parent stock has been lost sight of. A new breed might be obtained by judicious crossing, or even a single cross might bring an animal superior to either of its parents. These remarks are called forth by the fact that a cross-bred four-year-old, from a Hereford sire out of a Short-horn at the Smithfield, England, show, took the $150 cup as the best cross-bred, the $250 cup as the best steer, and the $500 cup as the best animal in the show. It is a well-established law of breeding that offspring take the good rather than the poor points of their parents, and right here lies the difference between Texas and northern cattle. By comparison, the Texans have but few points as good as the cattle of the north. Blooded bulls are seldom or never used in Texas. The consequence is that the Texans are now a distinct breed, never improving in quality, and according to the best judges, are deteriorating. On the other hand, northern stockgrowers have, as a rule, used full-blood or graded bulls. The consequence is that but for the one point of the Texans making better mothers, and even this is disputed, the northern cattle are far superior.
articles.summary: Argument for cross-breeding and blooded bulls, contrasting Texas and northern cattle.

articles.summary: J. A. Van Eegan returned from the east; his plug hat was shot full of holes.

articles.summary: Slaughter house and cold storage construction details.

articles.text: Dahl Bros., of Bismarck, are prepared to make suits on short notice. When in Bismarck, leave your measure with them and an order at any time will receive prompt attention. Repairing of all kinds promptly done and returned.

articles.text: John S. Warn, of the Oyster Grotto, is still in Bozeman. In a letter received from him this morning he states that he will remain there several days longer, but will return in due time to give the boys a good square meal, "on the dead square."
articles.summary: John S. Warn of the Oyster Grotto still in Bozeman.

articles.text: Frank Frankenberg, of the E 6 outfit, returned Monday from Springfield, Ohio, where he has been on a visit to his parents. He will leave for the E 6 ranch in a few days. Frank is a good guesser, winning one of Lorillard's $50 prizes in estimating the presidential vote.
articles.summary: Frank Frankenberg of the E 6 outfit returned from Ohio.

articles.text: Last Sunday morning the little Missouri began to rise rapidly. A gorge was formed above the bridge, and it seemed as if we were going to have a flood. The weather here was very cold, which probably was the cause of no damage being done, as the river was frozen over Sunday night. The present cold snap came in good time, as the refrigerator company still requires 600 tons to fill its houses.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri rose and gorged above the bridge but froze again; the refrigerator company still needs 600 tons of ice.

articles.text: It is to be hoped that all will take an interest in the shooting club, and practice for the contests. The winning score of last Friday's shoot should be the lowest average. The cold weather accounted for much of the poor shooting, but lack of practice accounted for much more. There are enough good shots on the river so that a formidable team could be organized and matches made with other teams up and down the line.
articles.summary: Call for practice and a shooting team.

articles.text: A preliminary meeting for the organization of a gun club was held last night in Roberts & Co.'s hall. Wm. Van Driesche was elected chairman and as but little business was to come before the meeting, the election of other officers was dispensed with. It was moved and carried that an executive committee of three, including the chairman of the meeting, be appointed to take charge of the shoot Saturday and that they should report next Wednesday evening at the same time and place, rules and regulation for succeeding shoots. The committee, as appointed, consists of Messrs. Packard, Paddock and Van Driesche. Now that the ball has been set rolling it is to be hoped that a lively interest will be aroused and that all interested in shooting will attend the meeting for permanent organization to be had next Wednesday evening at Roberts & Co.'s hall.
articles.summary: Preliminary gun club meeting at Roberts & Co.'s hall names a committee of Packard, Paddock and Van Driesche.

articles.summary: Williamson & Copeland finished their shop.

articles.text: Vic Smith was showing the tenderfoot how to shoot, in a back yard in Milwaukee, when a policeman put in an appearance and Vic had to pay $5 and costs in court. Vic can make lots more money shooting here than in Milwaukee. He is already pining for the Bad Lands, and will return soon.
articles.summary: Hunter Vic Smith fined in Milwaukee for shooting in a back yard.

articles.text: Joe O'Brien returned Friday night from a visit to relatives in Missouri and Iowa. He reports a complicated state of affairs in Iowa. A prohibition law was passed by a popular vote and, as it cannot be enforced, the saloon keepers are holding high carnival. They of course, can pay no license, and cannot be held responsible for selling to minors, etc., as the law does not recognize the right to sell liquor, and of course cannot punish any harm done from its effects.
articles.summary: Joe O'Brien returned from Missouri and Iowa and described Iowa prohibition.

articles.text: The Little Missouri river resembles the peace of God, "in that it passeth all understanding." The break-ups of course all come from the south as the river runs north. Perhaps for several days previous to our coldest days, there has been a chinook blowing near the head of the river. The water immediately begins running, and it depends upon the length of the thaw how far the water flows on the ice. If it meets cold weather it is liable to freeze up at any time. Thus there are formed several thicknesses of ice. South of the railroad crossing there are four thicknesses, north there are three, and twenty miles down the river there are but two. A curious circumstance was also noted yesterday. At McGregor's ranch down the river, the water was at least six inches deep on the top of the ice and flowing rapidly. Coming up the river to Wadsworth's ranch there was no sign of a thaw, the top ice being about two inches thick. Farther up the river solid ice was found in some places and in others only a thin crust. Some top crusts had no water under them and some had two feet and over.
articles.summary: Observations of layered ice and overflow on the Little Missouri, including water on the ice at McGregor's ranch.

articles.headline: The Shoot.
articles.text:
The weather was quite warm last Friday forenoon and it deceived all the shooters, as none were prepared for the cold weather of the afternoon. The consequence was that some very poor shooting was done. The contestants put in a dollar each, dividing the prizes into a first of six dollars and a second of four. A. T. Packard won first on a score of twenty one, and E. G. Paddock and J. N. Maxwell divided second on a score of twelve each. None of the scores do justice to the shooters, and succeeding winners must make a much higher score. The ranges were fifty, one hundred and two hundred yards. The fifty yard range had a two-inch bull's eye, the hundred yard a four-inch, and the two hundred a six inch. The rings were an inch and a quarter successively from the bull's eye. All the shooting was strictly off-hand, except that at two hundred yards, a body rest was allowed. The order of contestants was decided by lot, and the scores were as follows:

articles.headline: Mail Reform.
articles.text:
The transfer of the capital from Yankton to Bismarck, throws a large portion of of the more important mail matter passing between the Hills and the seat of government, over the northern route. At present such runs via Miles, and the service thereon is simply and utterly abominable. For instance matter mailed at Medora Jan. 15 reached us yesterday—twelve days after. Bismarck papers reach us four and five at a time, many days after publication and it is reasonable to suppose that letters are equally as long in transit. No regularly equipped stage line runs between the Hills and Miles, but in lieu thereforo a small buckboard outfit is operated between Spearfish and the railroad. A movement is on foot to secure a transfer of the mail service from the Miles City to the Medora route. A splendidly equipped stage line occupies the latter, making regular and quick trips, and if the change is made service will be expedited from two to five days. Petitions are circulating throughout the country and are extensively signed. It is hoped that the department will grant our reasonable request.—[Black Hills Times.

The same trouble is experinced in Medora. Papers and letters arrive here two or three weeks after the time of their leaving the Deadwood postoffice. All this delay would be dispensed with, had the Medora route the mail contract, and the desire of the people should be granted.
articles.summary: The Black Hills Times urges moving the Hills mail from the Miles City route to the Medora stage route; the Cow Boy agrees.
